title: The Twelfth Century
orientation: This chapter traces four intertwined twelfth-century developments -- the continuing conflict of Empire and papacy, the rise of the independent Lombard cities, the Crusades, and the growth of scholasticism -- as preparation for their culmination in the thirteenth century. It matters because it introduces the first generation of properly scholastic philosophers (Roscelin, Abelard, Saint Bernard, John of Salisbury) and shows how increasing papal power, urban commercial growth, and the recovery of Aristotle through translation together produced the intellectual conditions for the High Middle Ages.
historical_background: Russell frames the twelfth century as a transitional stage whose four central movements -- imperial-papal conflict, the rise of Lombard city republics, the Crusades, and scholasticism -- all culminate only in the thirteenth century, but are all, he stresses, bound up with the growth of ecclesiastical power. He notes the curious paradox that all parties (Emperor, papacy, Lombard cities, scholastics, Crusaders) justified their genuinely novel positions through appeals to ancient precedent, even though only the Emperor's appeal to old feudal and Roman forms corresponded to declining reality; the cities and the scholastics were, despite their own claims to be merely continuing old traditions, deeply original.
philosophical_problems: The problem of universals as newly sharpened by the rediscovery that Plato and Aristotle disagree about it (Roscelin's nominalism vs. William of Champeaux's realism vs. Abelard's intermediate position)
Whether dialectic (syllogistic reasoning) alone, apart from Scripture, is a sufficient road to truth (Abelard's position, and its limits)
Whether religious truth is best sought through reasoning or through subjective mystical experience and contemplation (Abelard vs. Saint Bernard)
Whether the Trinity can be rationally demonstrated without revelation (Anselm and Abelard both thought so, while remaining formally orthodox)

philosophers_discussed.name: Roscelin
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The first strict scholastic philosopher (b. ca. 1050); taught Abelard; accused of heresy over his view of the Trinity (that the Three Persons are three distinct substances) and forced to recant at Rheims in 1092; held, in Anselm's report, that universals are mere 'flatus vocis' ('breath of the voice'), making him some sort of nominalist.

philosophers_discussed.name: Abelard
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Roscelin's pupil (1079-1142), far abler and more famous, remembered both for his romance with Heloise (which ended in his castration by her uncle) and for his major works 'Sic et Non' and his treatment of universals; held that we predicate words-as-meaning of things, not things themselves, thereby steering a course between Roscelin's crude nominalism and William of Champeaux's realism, while still allowing Platonic ideas a place as God's own concepts.

philosophers_discussed.name: William of Champeaux
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A realist teacher of Abelard in Paris, whose views on universals Abelard combated and compelled him to modify.

philosophers_discussed.name: Saint Bernard of Clairvaux
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Leader of the twelfth-century mystical movement, Cistercian abbot of Clairvaux from 1115; brought unjust accusations of heresy against Abelard, secured his condemnation at Sens in 1141; hugely influential in ecclesiastical politics (combating antipopes and heresy, preaching the Second Crusade); sought religious truth in subjective contemplation rather than reasoning, and wrote Latin hymns of real beauty despite Russell's judgment that his saintliness 'did not suffice to make him intelligent.'

philosophers_discussed.name: John of Salisbury
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Not an important original thinker but valuable as a witness to his times; secretary to three archbishops of Canterbury (including Becket); called himself an 'Academic' (skeptic) in matters outside the faith; admired Abelard but laughed at his and Roscelin's theories of universals; still regarded Plato as 'the prince of all philosophers.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Arnold of Brescia
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A saintly heretic who held that clergy owning property could not be saved, and supported the Roman popular movement for communal liberty against the Pope; burned by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa's forces, with his ashes thrown into the Tiber to prevent relic-veneration.

schools_discussed: Early scholasticism (nominalism vs. realism on universals)
The School of Chartres (a humanistic movement admiring antiquity and following Plato and Boethius)

core_concepts.name: The medieval problem of universals (Roscelin, William of Champeaux, Abelard)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: When we call several different cats 'cats,' what, if anything, corresponds to the general word 'cat' itself? Roscelin said a universal like 'cat' is just a word, a puff of breath, with no reality beyond the individual cats. William of Champeaux, a realist, held universals have their own independent reality. Abelard, Roscelin's pupil, argued for a middle position: we do not predicate a bare physical word-sound of things, but a word as meaning; things genuinely resemble one another, and this resemblance gives rise to universals, but the resemblance itself is not a 'thing.' He also allowed that universals exist as patterns in God's mind prior to creation.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The scholastic debate over the ontological status of general terms (genera and species): whether they denote real, independently existing entities (realism), are mere names/vocal sounds with no corresponding reality (nominalism), or occupy some intermediate status as concepts grounded in real resemblances among particulars (Abelard's conceptualist-leaning position).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the central metaphysical/logical dispute of early scholasticism, made newly urgent by the twelfth-century discovery that Plato and Aristotle disagree about it, and it recurs, in more developed form, throughout the following two centuries of scholastic philosophy (Aquinas, Duns Scotus, Occam).
core_concepts.historical_origin: Sharpened in the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries by Roscelin's controversial nominalism and Anselm's and Abelard's responses to it.
examples: Roscelin's charge that a universal is mere 'flatus vocis,' a physical event of speech
Abelard's reply that a 'flatus vocis' is itself a thing, so what is predicated must be the word as meaning, not the word as physical sound
Abelard's view that Platonic ideas exist as God's own concepts, patterns for creation, even though universals as such are not independently existing things
objections: Anselm's charge (against Roscelin) that if a universal is only a vocal event, then 'man' would not be a real unity but only a common name, an unacceptably extreme atomistic consequence
John of Salisbury 'laughed at' both Abelard's and Roscelin's theories of universals, suggesting contemporaries found neither fully satisfying
competing_positions: William of Champeaux's realism (universals have independent reality)
Roscelin's nominalism (universals are mere words/vocal sounds)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell judges Abelard's treatment 'certainly very able,' remarking that 'the most modern discussions of the problem of universals have not got much further'; the debate directly anticipates Aquinas's, Duns Scotus's, and Occam's later treatments.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Roscelin's nominalist leanings got him into theological trouble over the Trinity, since treating the Three Persons as three distinct substances risked tritheism.

core_concepts.name: Scholasticism's defining characteristics
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell identifies four hallmarks of scholastic philosophy as it takes shape in the twelfth century: it stays within the bounds of orthodoxy (retracting views condemned by Church councils, much as a lower court submits to an appellate court); it increasingly treats Aristotle, not Plato, as the supreme authority; it places great weight on dialectic and syllogistic reasoning, making the general temper minute and disputatious rather than mystical; and it is preoccupied, though not exclusively, with the problem of universals once Aristotle's and Plato's disagreement on the topic became clear.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Russell's four-part characterization of scholasticism as a philosophical school: bounded orthodoxy, growing Aristotelian authority, reliance on dialectical/syllogistic method, and (among other concerns) the problem of universals.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It sets the interpretive frame for the entire scholastic period covered across this and the following several chapters, and identifies the defects Russell attributes to the method: indifference to facts and empirical science, over-reliance on reasoning where only observation could decide, and excessive attention to verbal subtlety.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Emerges, in Russell's account, with Roscelin as 'the first philosopher who can be regarded as strictly a scholastic,' early in the twelfth century.
examples: Roscelin's and Abelard's willingness to recant condemned views at Church councils rather than persist in heresy
Abelard's 'Sic et Non,' arguing both sides of many theological questions purely through dialectic
objections: Russell's own criticism that these methodological defects (over-reliance on reasoning, neglect of observation, verbal hairsplitting), already present in Plato, appear in the scholastics 'in a much more extreme form'
competing_positions: The rival mystical approach of Saint Bernard and his followers, which sought truth through contemplation rather than dialectic
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Defines the method that reaches its highest development in the thirteenth century with Aquinas, covered in the following chapters.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Scholastic philosophers were all clerics, subject to discipline by Church councils, and Russell suggests their sense of participating in the Church's political triumph stimulated their intellectual confidence.

core_concepts.name: Abelard's 'Sic et Non' and the value of dialectic
core_concepts.plain_explanation: In 'Sic et Non' ('Yes and No'), Abelard laid out dialectical arguments on both sides of many theological questions, often without resolving them, apparently valuing the exercise of disputation itself as sharpening the intellect. He held that, apart from Scripture, dialectic is the sole road to truth, and that nothing outside Scripture -- not even Apostles or Church Fathers -- is infallible.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Abelard's 1121-22 work presenting opposed authoritative quotations and arguments on a wide range of theological questions, used pedagogically to train critical, disputatious reasoning rather than to hand down settled doctrine.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It had, in Russell's words, 'a valuable effect as a solvent of prejudices and an encouragement to the fearless use of the intellect,' helping to wake people from 'dogmatic slumbers,' even though Russell notes 'no empiricist' could accept Abelard's claim that dialectic alone (barring Scripture) is the sole road to truth.
examples: Abelard's derivation of Logic's dignity from the opening of Saint John's Gospel ('In the beginning was the Logos')
objections: Russell's judgment that valuing logic as 'pre-eminently the Christian science' is, from a modern standpoint, excessive
competing_positions: Saint Bernard's mysticism, which sought truth in contemplation rather than disputation
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Contributed to Abelard's repeated condemnations for unorthodoxy (Soissons 1121, Sens 1141), driven, Russell suggests, more by his personal combativeness than by genuine heresy.

arguments.title: Abelard's account of universals as resemblance-based predication
premises: We do not predicate a thing of another thing; we predicate a word
Against Roscelin: a spoken word ('flatus vocis') is itself a physical thing, so what is predicated cannot be the word as mere sound
Therefore what is predicated must be the word as meaning
Things resemble each other, and these resemblances give rise to universal terms
The point of resemblance between two similar things is not itself a further thing (this, Abelard says, is realism's mistake)
arguments.conclusion: Universals are meaningful words applied to things in virtue of real resemblances among those things, but the resemblance itself, and the universal term, are not independently existing entities.
arguments.explanation: Abelard threads a path between Roscelin's crude nominalism (universal as mere vocal noise) and William of Champeaux's realism (universal as an independently real entity), while still preserving a role for Platonic ideas as patterns existing in God's mind prior to creation.
objections: Russell notes this raises the difficulty of what exactly a 'point of resemblance' is, if not itself some kind of entity
implications: Anticipates later, more technical treatments of universals as involving real similarity relations without positing free-standing abstract objects

arguments.title: Anselm's charge against Roscelin's nominalism
premises: According to Roscelin, a whole made up of parts has no reality of its own beyond the parts; the whole is a mere word
Applied to human beings, this implies 'man' is not a real unity but only a common name
Applied to the Trinity, this implies the Three Persons are three distinct substances
arguments.conclusion: Roscelin's nominalism, if taken consistently, risks tritheism (treating Father, Son, and Holy Ghost as effectively three Gods) and an untenable atomism about ordinary objects.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this largely as Anselm's polemical reconstruction of Roscelin's actual, poorly-documented views (since almost none of Roscelin's own writing survives), noting Roscelin recanted the Trinitarian implications at Rheims in 1092.
objections: Russell doubts that Roscelin held anything as 'foolish' as the literal 'flatus vocis' reading, suggesting Anselm's polemic may overstate the position
implications: Shows how abstract logical/metaphysical positions on universals carried immediate and dangerous theological consequences in this period

key_distinctions: Nominalism (Roscelin) vs. realism (William of Champeaux) vs. Abelard's intermediate resemblance-based account of universals
Dialectic/reasoning (Abelard) vs. subjective contemplation (Saint Bernard) as routes to religious truth
Literary archaism (claimed continuity with the past) vs. actual political/intellectual originality, which Russell says characterizes nearly all twelfth-century movements except the Emperor's cause
The spiritual function of the papacy (which Bernard insisted on) vs. its actual worldly, military, and political exercise (which Bernard criticized even while reinforcing papal authority)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: The renewed twelfth-century debate on universals directly continues the ancient disagreement Russell has already traced between Plato (universals as prior to things) and Aristotle (with two, partly conflicting, views of his own); the School of Chartres explicitly followed Plato and Boethius, continuing the earlier, largely Platonic-Augustinian cast of Western Christian philosophy described in prior chapters.
connections_to_later_philosophers: The problem of universals as posed here by Roscelin, William of Champeaux, and Abelard is picked up again in more developed form by Aquinas, Duns Scotus, and William of Occam in the chapters that follow; the recovery of Aristotle's logical works (Analytics, Topics, Sophistici Elenchi) via James of Venice and others in this chapter sets up the fuller Aristotelian revival of the thirteenth century.
political_social_context: The chapter ties scholasticism, the Crusades, and the rise of the Lombard cities all to the broader struggle for power between the papacy and lay rulers (chiefly the Emperor, but also France and England); the defeat of Frederick Barbarossa by the Lombard League (culminating at Legnano, 1176) marks the durable emergence of independent, commercially prosperous city-republics as a genuinely new political form, distinct from both declining feudalism and papal power.
religion_science_culture_context: The First Crusade (proclaimed by Urban II at Clermont, 1095) produced both a surge of religious enthusiasm that increased papal power and 'atrocious pogroms of Jews'; the Crusades also stimulated literary and scholarly contact with Constantinople, driving a wave of Greek-to-Latin translation via Constantinople, Palermo, and especially Toledo (where Archbishop Raymond's college of translators was particularly fruitful), which fed directly into the growth of scholasticism.
russell_presentation: Russell presents the twelfth century as a genuinely creative period that did not recognize its own originality, since every party (Emperor, papacy, Lombard cities, scholastics, Crusaders) legitimized itself by appeal to supposed ancient precedent even while doing something new. He is admiring of the intellectual daring of early scholastics like Abelard, praising his treatment of universals as still philosophically respectable by modern standards, while criticizing the scholastic method's characteristic defects (excessive trust in dialectic over observation, verbal hairsplitting) as more extreme than in Plato. Russell is notably unsympathetic to Saint Bernard, whom he credits with genuine religious feeling and fine Latin hymns but faults for intelligence, unfairness to Abelard, and a naive view of Crusading war as sustainable by religious enthusiasm alone -- captured in Russell's pointed remark, quoting the Encyclopaedia Britannica, that Bernard's greatness 'lay not in the qualities of his intellect, but of his character.'
critical_context: Common scholarly criticism: some historians of medieval philosophy argue Russell's brief treatment somewhat underplays how central and technically sophisticated Abelard's broader logical and ethical work (e.g. on intention in ethics) was beyond the specific universals debate covered here, and that his account of Roscelin, reconstructed almost entirely from hostile witnesses (Anselm, Abelard), should be treated with more caution than Russell's confident paraphrase suggests.
key_takeaways: Four bound-together twelfth-century developments -- imperial-papal conflict, the rise of the Lombard cities, the Crusades, and scholasticism -- all culminate in the thirteenth century.
Roscelin, the first strict scholastic, held a nominalist view of universals that got him into trouble over the Trinity; he recanted at Rheims in 1092.

Abelard, Roscelin's pupil, offered a more sophisticated intermediate account: universals are meaningful words applied on the basis of real resemblances, not independently existing entities, though Platonic ideas survive as concepts in God's mind.
Scholasticism's four hallmarks, per Russell, are bounded orthodoxy, growing Aristotelian authority, reliance on dialectic, and preoccupation (though not exclusive) with universals.

Saint Bernard led a rival mystical current, prioritizing contemplation over reasoning, and was instrumental (via his opposition to Abelard and his preaching of the Second Crusade) in expanding papal power despite personally deploring the papacy's worldliness.

Twelfth-century translation activity, centered on Toledo, Palermo, and Constantinople, steadily increased Western access to Aristotle's works, setting up the fuller recovery covered in later chapters.
study_notes:
This chapter is best read as connective tissue: it does not present one dominant philosophical system (as the Aquinas chapter will) but rather shows the institutional and intellectual scaffolding being erected -- cathedral schools evolving into universities, translation programs recovering more of Aristotle, and the terms of the universals debate being set -- that the thirteenth century will build on. Keep track of the running theme of disguised originality: Russell repeatedly notes that every twelfth-century party dressed up its genuinely new claims in the clothing of ancient precedent, a pattern worth watching for as you read later chapters on the Renaissance and Reformation, where a similar 'return to the ancients' rhetoric will mask real innovation.

The Abelard-Bernard contrast is worth studying closely as a paired case: Abelard represents confident, sometimes reckless, reliance on dialectical reason applied even to sacred doctrine, while Bernard represents an equally confident insistence that ultimate religious truth is reached only through contemplative experience, not argument. Russell judges both figures 'perhaps equally one-sided' -- a useful reminder that his sympathies (generally with reason over mysticism) do not prevent him crediting real limitations on the rationalist side too.

Finally, note how thin and indirect the twelfth century's knowledge of Aristotle still was: only the logical works were available in this period (Posterior Analytics found 'difficult'), and translations of substantive works like the Phaedo and Meno (by Henry Aristippus) 'had no immediate effect.' The fuller Aristotelian corpus -- and the crisis of interpretation it would provoke -- belongs to the following two chapters.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The method of arriving at truth through structured argument and counter-argument, question and answer, rather than through direct observation or mystical experience.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In scholastic usage, the technique of formal, syllogistic argumentation applied to theological and philosophical questions, central to the scholastic method and exemplified by Abelard's 'Sic et Non.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The view that general terms like 'cat' or 'man' are just names or words, without any independently existing reality corresponding to them.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The philosophical position, associated in this chapter with Roscelin, that universals have no reality beyond individual particulars and the words used to group them; contrasted with realism.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The view that general categories like 'cat' or 'man' are real things in their own right, not just names.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The scholastic position, associated with William of Champeaux, that universals possess a mind-independent reality distinct from, and prior to, the particular things that instantiate them.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Latin for 'breath of the voice'; Roscelin's supposed description of universals as mere vocal sounds with no further reality.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The phrase Anselm attributes to Roscelin to characterize his nominalist claim that a universal is nothing more than the physical event of uttering a word.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: An alliance of independent Northern Italian cities, led by Milan, that resisted the Holy Roman Emperor and allied with the Pope.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A military and political league of North Italian communes formed to resist Emperor Frederick Barbarossa's assertions of overlordship, defeating him decisively at Legnano in 1176.

questions.prompt: What four twelfth-century developments does Russell identify as especially significant, and what do they have in common?
questions.answer: The continued conflict of Empire and papacy, the rise of the Lombard cities, the Crusades, and the growth of scholasticism. Russell argues all four are intimately bound up with the increase of papal and ecclesiastical power, and all four culminate (rather than merely continuing) in the thirteenth century.
questions.explanation: This framing sets up both this chapter and the next, which treats the thirteenth-century culmination of the same movements.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher is described as 'the first philosopher who can be regarded as strictly a scholastic,' and what heretical view got him into trouble?
questions.answer: Roscelin, whose nominalist view of universals, applied to the Trinity, implied that the Three Persons are three distinct substances -- risking tritheism; he recanted at a council at Rheims in 1092.
questions.explanation: Almost nothing of Roscelin's own writing survives; his views are known mainly through Anselm's and Abelard's polemical reports.

questions.prompt: Compare Roscelin's, William of Champeaux's, and Abelard's positions on universals.
questions.answer: Roscelin (nominalist) held universals are mere words, 'flatus vocis,' with no reality beyond the utterance. William of Champeaux (realist) held universals have independent reality. Abelard took an intermediate position: we predicate the word as meaning (not as physical sound), grounded in real resemblances among particular things, while still allowing that Platonic ideas exist as patterns in God's mind prior to creation -- so universals as such are not free-standing things, but resemblance and divine ideas are not nothing either.
questions.explanation: Russell praises Abelard's position as still philosophically respectable, saying modern discussions 'have not got much further.'

questions.prompt: What is 'Sic et Non,' and what did Abelard intend by writing it?
questions.answer: 'Sic et Non' ('Yes and No'), composed 1121-22, presents dialectical arguments for and against a wide variety of theological theses, often without reaching a conclusion; Abelard seems to have valued the disputation itself as sharpening the intellect, and the book had the effect of waking people from dogmatic complacency.
questions.explanation: Abelard held that, apart from Scripture, dialectic is the sole road to truth -- a view Russell notes no empiricist could accept, though he credits it with valuable effect as a 'solvent of prejudices.'

questions.prompt: How did Saint Bernard contribute to Abelard's downfall, and what does Russell think of the fairness of his accusations?
questions.answer: Bernard, who failed to understand Abelard, accused him of treating the Trinity like an Arian, grace like a Pelagian, and the Person of Christ like a Nestorian, and of destroying the merit of faith by claiming God could be completely understood by reason. Russell states plainly that Abelard never actually maintained this last claim and always left a large province to faith; he suggests it was Abelard's combativeness, more than genuine heresy, that provoked Bernard's hostility and secured his condemnation at Sens in 1141.
questions.explanation: This illustrates Russell's broader skepticism toward Bernard's judgment despite acknowledging his genuine religious sincerity.

questions.prompt: What paradox does Russell identify in how twelfth-century parties (Emperor, papacy, Lombard cities, scholastics, Crusaders) justified their positions?
questions.answer: All parties appealed to supposedly ancient precedent to justify what were, in fact, genuinely novel positions -- the Emperor to feudal and Roman tradition, the papacy partly to the forged Donation of Constantine, the cities to republican Rome, the scholastics to Scripture or Plato/Aristotle, the Crusaders to restoring the pre-Islamic status quo. Only the Emperor's appeal actually matched declining reality (feudalism truly was decaying), which is part of why the imperial cause ultimately failed while the others, despite their archaistic rhetoric, proved genuinely creative.
questions.explanation: Russell calls this pattern 'disguised originality,' visible in both twelfth-century politics and thought.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Abelard's argument against Roscelin's claim that a universal is mere 'flatus vocis.'
questions.answer: Abelard points out that a 'flatus vocis' (a spoken word as a physical, acoustic event) is itself a thing -- so if universals were merely that, they would just be particular physical events, which cannot be what is genuinely predicated across many different objects. Instead, what we predicate must be the word taken as meaning, appealing to Aristotle's authority; and things genuinely resemble each other, giving rise to universal terms, though the resemblance itself is not a separate 'thing' (which Abelard identifies as realism's mistake).
questions.explanation: This is the core move by which Abelard distinguishes his own account from both Roscelin's crude nominalism and William of Champeaux's realism.

flashcards.front: What four twelfth-century developments does Russell single out for discussion?
flashcards.back: The conflict of Empire and papacy, the rise of the Lombard cities, the Crusades, and the growth of scholasticism.

flashcards.front: Who is described as 'the first philosopher who can be regarded as strictly a scholastic'?
What does 'flatus vocis' mean, and who used it to describe universals?
flashcards.back: 'Breath of the voice'; used (per Anselm) to describe Roscelin's nominalist claim that a universal is just a spoken sound.

flashcards.front: Who were Abelard's teacher and pupil-turned-lover mentioned in the chapter?
flashcards.back: William of Champeaux was his realist teacher (whom he opposed); Heloise was his lover, niece of Canon Fulbert.

flashcards.front: What happened to Abelard after his affair with Heloise was discovered?
flashcards.back: Canon Fulbert had him castrated; Abelard retired to a monastery at St. Denis, Heloise to a nunnery at Argenteuil.

flashcards.front: What is Abelard's most famous book, and what does its title mean?
flashcards.back: 'Sic et Non' ('Yes and No'), composed 1121-22, giving dialectical arguments for and against many theological theses.

flashcards.front: What was Abelard's solution to the problem of universals?
flashcards.back: We predicate the word as meaning (not as physical sound); universals arise from real resemblances among things, though the resemblance itself is not a separate thing; Platonic ideas survive as God's own concepts.

flashcards.front: Who led the twelfth-century mystical movement and founded the abbey of Clairvaux?
What did Saint Bernard do to oppose Abelard?
flashcards.back: He accused Abelard of multiple heresies and secured his condemnation, first informally and then formally at the Council of Sens in 1141.

flashcards.front: Who called himself an 'Academic' and is valued mainly as a witness to twelfth-century intellectual life?
What was the School of Chartres known for?
flashcards.back: A humanistic movement admiring antiquity, following Plato and Boethius, with renewed interest in mathematics (e.g. Adelard of Bath's translation of Euclid).

flashcards.front: Which three cities were the main sources of Greek-to-Latin translation in the twelfth century?
flashcards.back: Constantinople, Palermo, and Toledo (Toledo being the most important, though often via Arabic rather than direct from Greek).

quiz.prompt: Which four movements does Russell identify as the special interest of the twelfth century?
options: The Reformation, the Renaissance, the printing press, and the discovery of America
The conflict of Empire and papacy, the rise of the Lombard cities, the Crusades, and the growth of scholasticism
The Norman Conquest, the Investiture Controversy, the Great Schism, and the Black Death
The founding of Cluny, the First Crusade, the Magna Carta, and the Hundred Years' War
quiz.explanation: Russell opens the chapter by naming these four aspects as specially interesting, noting all culminate in the thirteenth century.

options: Saint Anselm
Roscelin
Abelard
Saint Bernard

options: True
False

quiz.prompt: According to Abelard, what do we actually predicate when we apply a universal term to different things?

The word taken as meaning, grounded in real resemblances among the things

He was castrated by Canon Fulbert and retired to a monastery

That most parties justified genuinely new positions by appealing to (real or forged) ancient precedent, even though, except for the Emperor's cause, their situations did not actually match the past
That no one at the time could read or write

options: Venice
Rome

quiz.prompt: Match each figure to their defining role in this chapter: (1) Roscelin, (2) Abelard, (3) Saint Bernard, (4) John of Salisbury.
options: (1) First strict scholastic and nominalist on universals; (2) Wrote Sic et Non and refined the theory of universals; (3) Led the twelfth-century mystical movement and opposed Abelard; (4) Chronicled the age and called himself an 'Academic'
(1) Led the mystical movement; (2) First strict scholastic; (3) Chronicler of the age; (4) Wrote Sic et Non
(1) Chronicler of the age; (2) Led the mystical movement; (3) Wrote Sic et Non; (4) First strict scholastic
(1) Wrote Sic et Non; (2) Led the mystical movement; (3) First strict scholastic; (4) Chronicler of the age
quiz.explanation: Roscelin pioneers scholasticism and nominalism, Abelard develops the theory of universals in Sic et Non and elsewhere, Bernard leads twelfth-century mysticism and opposes Abelard, and John of Salisbury is valued as a witness to the intellectual life of the age.

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Abelard's dialectical approach to religious truth with Saint Bernard's mystical, contemplative approach. Which does Russell seem to find more philosophically defensible, and why does he nonetheless call them 'perhaps equally one-sided'?
rubric: Accurately states both Abelard's and Bernard's positions
Identifies specific textual evidence (Sic et Non, Bernard's condemnation of Abelard, Bernard's hymns)

essay_prompts.prompt: Explain the twelfth-century debate over universals among Roscelin, William of Champeaux, and Abelard, and assess Russell's claim that Abelard's treatment remains philosophically respectable by modern standards.
rubric: States each position (nominalism, realism, Abelard's intermediate view) accurately
Explains Abelard's argument against Roscelin using the flatus vocis point
Engages with Russell's evaluative claim about Abelard's lasting relevance
Well-organized and precise use of terminology
